title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

reading.body:
This is an impersonation failure built on synthetic media. An AI-generated video presented a well-known financial sector figure as endorsing an investment, and the victim treated the apparent endorsement as real. The fabricated video was the entry point, not the whole scheme. The fraud then moved to a private WhatsApp channel, where the victim was pressed to invest more, open multiple online accounts, and grant remote access to their computer on the claim that this was assistance with the investment.

Catching it at the advert stage would have required independently verifying who was actually behind the approach and confirming that the provider was authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, which is the check the Police Service of Northern Ireland advised. The remote access request is the point where the scheme stopped resembling an investment and became direct control of the victim's accounts and borrowing. Nothing in the reporting describes a technical detection step that flagged the video as generated.

What is not established: the celebrity in the video was never named, and the BBC's account of similar scams using other financial experts is reporting on other adverts, not a finding that those individuals endorsed anything. No arrest, charge or verdict is reported, and the identity of the fraudsters is unknown.

reports.title: Victim loses £250k after scammers use AI video of 'well-known' celebrity

summary:
A person in the Ards and north Down area lost £250,000 in an AI-related investment scam, according to the Police Service of Northern Ireland. The victim saw an AI-generated video that appeared to feature a well-known financial sector personality. The advert promoted an investment and promised significant returns. The PSNI did not name the celebrity. BBC News NI reported seeing similar scams that used financial experts such as Martin Lewis, Peter Jones and Steven Bartlett.

After a small initial investment, the victim was contacted on WhatsApp and urged to pay more. The fraudsters persuaded them to open multiple online accounts and gained remote access to their computer, saying they were helping with the investment. The victim was encouraged to borrow money, and the funds went to accounts controlled by criminals. Police called it a sophisticated and substantial fraud. They advised people to independently verify who they deal with and check that financial services providers are authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority. Superintendent Joanne Gibson urged people to stop and check and encouraged families to talk to relatives about fraud.
